procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Calcutta in its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction Matter No. 157 of 1951.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated the 23rd day of August, 1951, of the High Court of Calcutta in its Ordinary Original Civil Jurisdiction Matter No. 157 of 1951, passed on an application under section 34 of the Arbitration Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent took an appeal to the Appellate Division of the High Court from the judgment of a single Judge sitting on the Original Side of that Court. A bench consisting of Chakravartti C. J. and Sarkar J. heard the appeal. By two separate judgments which concurred in the result, the Chief Justice and the other learned Judge allowed the appeal and vacated the order for stay.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant has come to the Supreme Court on the strength of a certificate under article 133 ( 1) (a) of the Constitution, against the judgment of an appellate bench of the Calcutta High Court, ·dated the 24th February, 1953, reversing, on appeal, the judgment and order of a single Judge sitting on the Original Side of that Court.

directions: Case sent back for the decision of the question whether the respondent was or was not a party to the arbitration agreement.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is incumbent upon a court, when considering an application to stay a suit under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, to first decide the question of whether a binding arbitration agreement exists between the parties to the suit.

facts: A party to a lawsuit applied to the court for a stay of the legal proceedings under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act.
The other party (the plaintiff) disputed that they were a party to the contract containing the arbitration clause, arguing the contract was with a third party.
The core issue before the court was whether it had to first resolve the dispute about the existence of a binding arbitration agreement before it could grant the stay.
law: Section 34 of the Arbitration Act allows a court to stay a legal proceeding if certain conditions are met.
The first and most essential condition for granting a stay is that a binding arbitration agreement must exist between the parties to the suit.
The question of whether a party is bound by an arbitration agreement is a jurisdictional issue that must be decided by the court, not the arbitrator.
application: The Supreme Court stated that it is "incumbent upon the Court" to "decide first of all" whether a binding arbitration agreement exists between the parties when an application for a stay is made.
The Court described this as the "first and essential pre-requisite" for making a stay order under Section 34.
The Court reasoned that the question of whether the dispute falls within the scope of an arbitration clause presupposes that such an agreement actually exists between the parties.
It held that the court to which the application is made must review the facts and evidence to "make up its mind whether the arbitrator has jurisdiction or not."
Therefore, the party applying for the stay must successfully establish that the other party is, in fact, a party to the arbitration agreement before the court can proceed to grant the stay.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it is mandatory for a court, when considering an application to stay a suit under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, to first determine whether a binding arbitration agreement exists between the parties involved in the lawsuit.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is incumbent upon a court, when considering an application to stay a suit under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, to first decide the question of whether a binding arbitration agreement exists between the parties to the suit.
appellant_arguments: The court must first decide the question of whether the respondent was a party to the arbitration agreement as an issue within the Section 34 proceeding.

The appellant argued that the respondent was indeed a party to the contract (and thus the arbitration agreement), despite being described as a broker, because under Indian law, an agent contracting on behalf of an undisclosed principal is liable.
If the court finds that the respondent is a party to the agreement, the suit must be stayed to allow arbitration to proceed.
respondent_arguments: The court should not decide the question of whether a binding arbitration agreement exists in a preliminary proceeding under Section 34.

This is because the question of whether the respondent is a party to the contract is the main issue in the suit itself, and a decision in the stay application would prejudice the parties and create a bar of res judicata.
On the merits, the respondent argued they were merely a broker or intermediary, not a contracting party, and therefore could not be bound by the arbitration clause.

cases.principle: Where an application is made under section 34 of the Arbitration Act to stay a suit, and an issue is raised about the formation, existence, or validity of the contract containing the arbitration clause, the court is not required to refuse a stay. Instead, the court has the discretion to decide the issue of the arbitration agreement's existence or validity, even if it means incidentally deciding on the validity or existence of the parent contract.

cases.case_name: A. M. Mair and Co. v. Gordhandas Sagarmull
cases.principle: A dispute relating to the rights and liabilities of parties based on the contract itself falls within the purview of a widely worded arbitration clause.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When an application is made to stay a suit under an arbitration act, and an issue is raised as to the formation, existence, or validity of the arbitration agreement between the parties to the suit, the court must first decide whether a binding arbitration agreement exists. This determination is an essential prerequisite to ordering a stay, as the question of whether a party is bound by an arbitration agreement cannot be decided by the arbitrators.
obiter: The question of whether the dispute in a suit falls within the scope of an arbitration clause presupposes the existence of a binding arbitration agreement between the parties.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: It is incumbent upon the court, when considering an application to stay a suit under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, to first decide the question of whether a binding arbitration agreement exists between the parties. Where an issue is raised as to the formation, existence, or validity of the contract containing the arbitration clause, the court is not bound to refuse a stay but may, on the application for stay, decide the issue as to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement, even though it may involve incidentally a decision as to the existence of the parent contract.
legal_tests_applied: For a stay to be granted under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, the court must be satisfied that: (1) The proceeding was commenced by a party to an arbitration agreement against another party to the agreement; (2) The legal proceeding sought to be stayed is in respect of a matter agreed to be referred; (3) The applicant for stay is a party to the legal proceeding, has taken no step in the proceeding after appearance, and was and is ready and willing to arbitrate; and (4) There is no sufficient reason why the matter should not be referred to arbitration in accordance with the agreement.
policy_considerations: If a court were to refuse to stay an action simply because a party claims the arbitrator has no jurisdiction, such a claim would always defeat an agreement to submit disputes to arbitration, undermining the purpose of such agreements. The application for a stay provides the very opportunity for the court to determine whether the action should be stayed or not based on the facts and arguments presented.
